title: Morphemes — The Smallest Units of Meaning
description: How words break down into meaningful pieces

concepts.title: What Is a Morpheme?
concepts.contentHtml:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function. Words are built from one or more morphemes.

cat has one morpheme. cats has two: cat (the animal) + -s (plural). un-kind-ness has three: un- (negation) + kind (quality) + -ness (nominalizer).

Crucially, a morpheme is a unit of meaning, not of spelling or sound. The plural morpheme -s appears as three different sounds in English: /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, /ɪz/ in buses — yet linguists count them as the same morpheme.

concepts.title: Free vs Bound Morphemes
concepts.contentHtml:
A free morpheme can stand alone as a word: dog, run, happy. A bound morpheme must attach to another morpheme: -ing, -ed, un-, -tion cannot appear by themselves.

Most roots in English are free, but many languages build heavily with bound morphemes. Turkish is famously agglutinative: evlerinizden means 'from your (plural, formal) houses' — one word, four morphemes: ev (house) + -ler (plural) + -iniz (your, plural or formal) + -den (from).

Swahili similarly packs tense, subject, and object agreement into a single verb word.

concepts.title: Roots and Affixes
concepts.contentHtml:
The root is the core morpheme that carries the main lexical meaning. Affixes are bound morphemes that attach to roots.

Affixes by position:

  • Prefix — before the root: un-happy, re-write, mis-understand
  • Suffix — after the root: happi-ness, teach-er, quick-ly
  • Infix — inside the root (rare in English, common in Tagalog and Arabic)
  • Circumfix — wraps around the root (German past participle: ge-mach-t 'made')

English borrows roots from Latin and Greek heavily: bio- (life), -logy (study), graph- (write). Knowing roots unlocks vocabulary systematically.

title: Derivation and Inflection
description: Two ways affixes change words — and why the distinction matters

concepts.title: Inflectional Morphology
concepts.contentHtml:
Inflection tweaks a word's grammatical form without changing its core meaning or word class. English has eight inflectional suffixes:

  • Plural -s: cat → cats
  • Possessive -'s: cat → cat's
  • Third-person singular -s: run → runs
  • Past tense -ed: walk → walked
  • Progressive -ing: walk → walking
  • Past participle -en/-ed: eaten, walked
  • Comparative -er: fast → faster
  • Superlative -est: fast → fastest

Languages like Russian, Latin, and Arabic have far richer inflectional systems with gender, case, and aspect all marked on words.

concepts.title: Derivational Morphology
concepts.contentHtml:
Derivation creates a new word — often with a new meaning and/or word class. Adding -ness to an adjective makes a noun: dark → darkness. Adding -ize makes a verb: modern → modernize.

Derivational morphemes can stack: modern → modernize → modernization → anti-modernization. Each step builds on the last.

A key diagnostic: inflection is usually outermost (closest to the word's edge), while derivation is inner. In modernizations, the derivational chain (modern-ize-ation) sits inside the inflectional plural -s. You can't add plural before adding -ation.

concepts.title: Cross-Linguistic Variation in Inflection
concepts.contentHtml:
Languages vary enormously in how much they inflect. Analytic languages like Mandarin express grammatical relationships through word order and separate particles, not inflection. 'I yesterday market go' (我昨天去市场) requires no morphological marking for tense.

Synthetic languages pack grammatical information into words via inflection. Latin amat 'he/she loves' encodes person, number, tense, mood, and voice all in suffix -at. Polysynthetic languages like Inuktitut go further, condensing whole sentences into a single word-form.

Ferdinand de Saussure noted that what matters is not the form but the distinctions a system draws — the differences, not the substance.

title: Word Formation Processes
description: Beyond affixes — compounding, conversion, blending, and more

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.contentHtml:
Compounding joins two or more free morphemes into a new word: sun + flower = sunflower, over + look = overlook, tooth + paste = toothpaste.

The compound's meaning is often idiomatic — a greenhouse is not simply a green house. In English, the rightmost element (the head) determines the category: a bookworm is a worm (noun), an overripe is ripe (adjective).

German is famous for long compounds: Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung (speed limit) = Geschwindigkeit (speed) + Begrenzung (limitation). Mandarin compounds are similarly productive, building new words from existing characters: 电 (electricity) + 话 (speech) = 电话 (telephone).

concepts.title: Conversion and Blending
concepts.contentHtml:
Conversion (zero-derivation) changes a word's category with no overt morpheme: email (noun) → to email (verb); google became a verb. English is unusually productive at this: to bottle, to chair (a meeting), to friend (someone).

Blending merges parts of two words into one: smoke + fog = smog, breakfast + lunch = brunch, motor + hotel = motel, web + log = blog.

Clipping shortens a word: advertisement → ad, influenza → flu, telephone → phone. These processes constantly expand vocabulary without new affixes.

concepts.title: Reduplication and Infixation
concepts.contentHtml:
Reduplication — copying part or all of a morpheme — is a major process in many languages. In Tagalog, partial reduplication marks the future: bili (buy) → bibili (will buy). In Malay, full reduplication marks plurality: orang (person) → orang-orang (people).

Infixation inserts a morpheme inside the root. Tagalog has infixes: sulat (write) → s-um-ulat (wrote), where -um- is inserted. English uses expressive infixes informally: abso-blooming-lutely (a 'tmesis').

Arabic root-and-pattern morphology is a remarkable system: the root k-t-b (write) generates kataba (he wrote), kitaab (book), kaatib (writer) by mapping the consonants onto vowel templates.

title: Morphological Typology
description: How the world's languages classify by morphological structure

concepts.title: Isolating, Agglutinative, Fusional
concepts.contentHtml:
Linguists classify languages by how they combine morphemes:

  • Isolating (analytic): each word is typically one morpheme; grammar via word order. Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai.
  • Agglutinative: morphemes string together transparently, each with one function. Turkish, Swahili, Finnish, Japanese.
  • Fusional (inflecting): morphemes fuse so that one form expresses multiple categories. Latin -o in amo marks person (1st), number (singular), tense (present), mood (indicative) simultaneously.

These are prototypes on a continuum — most languages show mixed properties. English has moved from highly fusional (Old English) toward more analytic over 1,000 years.

concepts.title: Agglutination in Detail — Turkish and Swahili
concepts.contentHtml:
Agglutinative morphology is clean: morpheme boundaries are clear and each morpheme has one consistent meaning.

Turkish ev-ler-im-den 'from my houses': ev (house) + -ler (plural) + -im (my) + -den (from). Each suffix is distinct and predictable.

Swahili verb agreement is agglutinative: ni-ta-ki-soma 'I will read it' = ni- (I) + -ta- (future) + -ki- (it, class 7) + -soma (read). Subject, tense, and object agreement are all separate morphemes that stack.

This transparency makes agglutinative languages systematic to learn once you know the morpheme inventory, though the forms can grow long.

concepts.title: Noun Classes and Agreement Systems
concepts.contentHtml:
Many languages organize nouns into classes (or genders), requiring agreeing morphemes on verbs, adjectives, and determiners.

Bantu languages like Swahili have 15+ noun classes. Each class has a prefix that propagates to all agreeing words: m-toto m-dogo a-na-kula 'the small child is eating' — m- marks the person class on both noun and adjective, and a- marks it on the verb.

Most Romance languages have two genders (masculine/feminine); German has three (masculine/feminine/neuter). In Russian, all three genders take different case endings across six cases — yielding dozens of agreement paradigms. These systems show that morphology and syntax interlock tightly.

title: Morphology Meets Phonology and Syntax
description: Where morphemes interact with sound and sentence structure

concepts.title: Allomorphs — When Morphemes Change Shape
concepts.contentHtml:
An allomorph is one of the phonological forms a morpheme takes in different environments. The English plural morpheme has three allomorphs: /s/ (cats), /z/ (dogs), /ɪz/ (buses). The choice is determined automatically by the preceding sound — this is phonologically conditioned allomorphy.

English indefinite article: a vs an — the choice depends on whether the following word starts with a vowel sound. A cat but an apple, an hour (silent h), a university (starts with /j/ consonant sound).

Suppletive allomorphs are irregular: go / went, good / better. These are historically different words that got absorbed into the same paradigm — remnants of older, more complex systems.

concepts.title: Morphological Productivity and Blocking
concepts.contentHtml:
Productivity measures how freely a morpheme can form new words. -ness is highly productive: you can attach it to nearly any adjective to form a noun. -th (as in warmth) is unproductive — you can't form *coolth.

Blocking occurs when an existing word prevents a new derivation from being created. You can't say *furiosity because fury already occupies the slot. The existing form blocks the new formation.

Blocking reflects the mental lexicon's organization — knowing a word preempts deriving it. This links morphology to the cognitive study of language production.

concepts.title: Clitics and the Morphology–Syntax Interface
concepts.contentHtml:
Clitics are elements that behave like words syntactically but attach phonologically to a host. English 's (possessive) and contracted auxiliaries like 'll and 've (I'll, you've) are clitics — they can't stand alone but are syntactically freer than typical affixes.

The possessive in 'the Queen of England's crown' attaches to the last word of the whole phrase ('England'), not just the head noun. No ordinary affix could do that — it shows the possessive is a syntactic clitic riding on a phrase.

French subject clitics je, tu, il are similarly borderline: they are obligatory (more like affixes) but separable (more like words). The morphology–syntax boundary is genuinely blurry in many languages.
